metaDescription: Six small podcast mixers and interfaces compared on desk footprint, XLR inputs, monitoring and portability, for tight desks and travel kits.
expertTake: The FIFINE Ampligame SC3 is the best small podcast mixer here because it gives a real XLR input, a slider and a mute button in the smallest, simplest body. The MAONO E2 Gen2 is the value pick when a second host joins the desk. A show with three or more voices should skip small boards and buy a four input recorder.
introParagraphs: A small podcast mixer solves a very practical problem: a desk that already holds a monitor, a keyboard and a boom arm has little room left for a console. The best small boards keep the controls you touch constantly within reach and push everything else into software.

Size always costs something. Most compact units carry one or two real microphone inputs, simple preamps and few extras, so the useful question is which of those compromises your show can live with and which it cannot.

products.name: FIFINE Ampligame SC3 single XLR mixer with Indi-Fader
products.description:
The SC3 packs the three controls a solo host touches most into a compact box: a smooth slider, a mute button and a monitor button, all on the front where a hand finds them without looking. A single XLR input accepts a proper microphone, and USB plug and play means the computer sees a sound card immediately.

Its limits come with the size. There is one microphone input and no effects or recording, so a second voice means a second device. Beside the BOMGE mini 2 it offers a physical slider and mute button that a bare interface lacks, while the BOMGE offers two inputs and phantom power in a similar footprint.

The SC3 sits well at the edge of a desk or on a monitor riser. Use a short balanced XLR cable, route the USB lead along the back and keep the box away from a router or power brick that could add noise to the microphone path. Because the controls are few and clearly placed, the board stays out of the way during a long session. A small habit helps: tape a reference mark beside the slider at the position that gives your usual level, so a bumped control is obvious at a glance. If a second host joins later, the SC3 can stay on the desk as a backup box for travel.
products.bestFor: A solo host with a tight desk who wants physical controls and an XLR input.
pros: Slider, mute and monitor on the front
XLR input for a real microphone

products.name: BOMGE mini 2 channel USB audio interface with XLR and 48V
products.description:
BOMGE's mini interface is the smallest way to get two microphone connections and phantom power into a computer. It is closer to a pocket interface than a mixer, with gain knobs instead of faders and USB for both Mac and PC.

The tradeoff is hands on control. There is no slider or mute button, so level changes and muting happen in software, which suits an editor who works on a computer but not a live host. Next to the SC3 it adds a second input and phantom power but loses the front controls.

It travels very well. A laptop bag has room for it, and the interface needs no power supply beyond the USB port. Keep the gain knobs away from their extremes, use quality XLR cables and consider a pair of headphones that suit the monitoring output. A short USB lead with a right angle plug keeps the connector from snagging in a bag. Because the interface has no mute button, learn the shortcut in your recording software so you can cut the microphone quickly when a cough or a doorbell interrupts.
products.bestFor: Travelers and tight desks that need two mic inputs and phantom power.

products.name: MAONO E2 Gen2 dual XLR podcast mixer with loopback
products.description:
The E2 Gen2 keeps the desk footprint modest while carrying two XLR preamps, loopback, Bluetooth and eight customizable sound effects. It is the box for two hosts who do not have room for a console.

It is larger than a pocket interface but gives more control, with knobs and buttons that a pair of speakers can reach. There is no recording on the unit, so a computer is part of the setup. Against the SC3 it doubles the microphone inputs and adds loopback, at a higher price tier.

Place it between the two seats if you can, so each host reaches their own controls. Keep Bluetooth for a phone call and the effects for a jingle, and use balanced cables to keep the small preamps quiet. Sit the two microphones at equal distances from the mixer so each cable is the same length, and have both hosts speak at their natural volume while you set the gain. Matching levels at the source is the best defense, because a small box offers no individual faders to rebalance a louder partner.
products.bestFor: Two hosts who share a small desk and need loopback.
pros: Two XLR preamps in a small box

products.name: Kaschun 4 channel Bluetooth mixer with XLR and USB
products.description:
Kaschun's four channel mixer is a compact console with knobs and a seven band EQ, 99 DSP effects, 48V phantom power, Bluetooth and a USB audio interface. It looks like a real mixer in a size that still sits on a crowded desk.

It is larger than the pocket boards, and the channel count can mislead, because a four channel board does not promise four microphone inputs. Next to the E2 Gen2 it has more tone control but less clarity about its mic channels.

Use it when you want hands on EQ in a small package. Keep the effects light and listen for hiss at your working gain before an important recording. A seven band EQ is easy to overuse, so start with all bands flat, make one small cut where the room sounds boxy and compare against the flat setting before keeping it. Ask whether you really need four channels, because a smaller board might serve better.
products.bestFor: A small desk that wants an EQ and several input types.
pros: Seven band EQ in a compact console

products.name: SINWE live sound card audio mixer for podcast production
products.description:
SINWE's live sound card mixer is the cheapest way here to get a compact mixing board with a USB connection for podcasting. It is the small, all in one box style popular with streamers.

Details on preamps and gain are thin, so treat it as a starter board and test it with your microphone. Compared with the SC3 it offers more consumer style features but less clarity about the XLR path.

It suits a beginner who wants to try podcasting on a tiny budget. Keep expectations modest and plan to upgrade the microphone first. Record a minute of silence and listen at high volume to learn the noise floor, then decide whether the hiss is acceptable for your show. Boards in this tier often ship with small power adapters, so use a clean outlet and keep the adapter away from the microphone cable to avoid hum.
products.bestFor: A tight budget and a very small desk.

products.name: MAONO podcast bundle with audio mixer and 3.5mm mic
products.description:
This MAONO kit puts a mixer and microphone in one small station, supporting two people and four devices, with eight built in effects and four recordable ones. It is meant for a creator who wants a complete small setup in one purchase.

The microphone is a 3.5mm unit, which limits sound quality and upgrade options compared with XLR boards. Beside the E2 Gen2 it is more complete in the box but less capable of growing.

Use it for a quick start. Keep the microphone close to your mouth and consider an XLR upgrade later. A 3.5mm capsule drops off quickly with distance, so mark your talking position on the desk and stay there. The four recordable effects are best used for your own intro and outro clips, which gives a small show a produced feel without extra software.
products.bestFor: Beginners who want a complete small station in one box.
pros: Supports two people and four devices

buyingCriteria.explanation: The smallest boards save desk space by dropping controls. The BOMGE mini 2 has gain knobs only, while the SC3 keeps a slider and mute button within a small footprint. Decide which controls you touch during a session and keep those, because a missing mute button is the usual regret with tiny interfaces.

Small boards carry one or two real microphone inputs. The SC3 has one, while the BOMGE mini 2 and MAONO E2 Gen2 have two. Count the microphones you need at once, because a third voice will not fit on any of these without a second device. If a show occasionally adds a guest, a second small interface or a four input recorder is a cleaner fix than forcing one box to do more than it was designed for.

Condenser microphones need 48V. The BOMGE mini 2 lists it and the Kaschun does too. If you use a dynamic microphone, phantom is optional, but a board that provides it lets you change microphones later.

The BOMGE mini 2 is USB powered and fits a laptop bag, which suits travel and remote interviews. Desk boards like the E2 Gen2 and Kaschun want a stable surface. Choose based on whether the board will leave the studio.

A direct monitor control lets you hear yourself without delay. The SC3 has a monitor button, and interfaces vary. Without direct monitoring you hear the delay of the computer, which can make speech awkward.

A bundle like the MAONO kit saves research but includes a 3.5mm microphone that you will replace. If your desk is truly tight, think about the stand as well, since a boom arm clamped to the edge frees more surface than any change of mixer and keeps the microphone off the tabletop where thumps travel. A small board with an XLR input and a separate microphone grows with you.

howWeEvaluated.title: Footprint
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared how much desk each unit demands, from the pocket sized BOMGE mini 2 to the Kaschun console. Smaller is only better if the controls you need survive. We also looked at cable exits, because a box with jacks on the back and sides eats more desk depth than one with a clean front and rear layout.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked for sliders, mute buttons and monitor controls, favoring the SC3's front mounted set. A host reaches for mute during a cough and for volume during a lively moment, so those two controls matter more than a long list of effects tucked into a menu.

howWeEvaluated.title: Microphone path
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted XLR inputs and phantom power, noting two inputs on the BOMGE and E2 Gen2.

howWeEvaluated.title: Portability
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered USB power and weight for travel use. A unit that runs from a laptop port and fits a coat pocket scored higher than one that needs a wall adapter, since the best recording gear is the one you actually bring to the interview.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared price tiers, with the SINWE and BOMGE at the lowest and the E2 Gen2 higher.

cards.text: USB power, low weight and no external supply, so the box fits a laptop bag and works anywhere.

cards.text: The BOMGE mini 2 is the travel pick, and the SC3 works if you have space for a desk box.

maintenance.why: Small boards have small gaps that collect dust and crumbs from a busy desk. Use compressed air and a soft brush, and keep the board covered when it is not in use.
A loose plug drops audio. Replace worn cables.
Confirm the setting before connecting a condenser, and switch phantom off before unplugging a cable, since the voltage change can cause a loud pop in headphones.
Knobs drift when bumped. A quick test avoids a ruined take.
A pouch protects small knobs and jacks.

faq.q: What is the best small podcast mixer?
faq.a: The FIFINE Ampligame SC3 is the best for a solo host, and the MAONO E2 Gen2 suits two. Both are small enough for a crowded desk, and both appear to the computer as a sound card. If you travel often, the BOMGE mini 2 is smaller still and draws power from the USB port, though it leaves out a slider and a mute button.

faq.q: Can a small mixer record two people?
faq.a: Yes, if it has two XLR inputs, such as the BOMGE mini 2 or the E2 Gen2. Keep in mind that two people share one headphone feed on most small boards, so you may need a headphone splitter or amplifier. Place the microphones at similar distances and set gain with both people speaking naturally.

Size does not decide sound. Preamp quality matters more, and a small interface with a clean preamp can beat a large board with a noisy one. The bigger differences come from the microphone, the room and the distance between mouth and capsule, which is why a pop filter and a boom arm help more than extra inches of mixer.
Only for condenser microphones. Dynamic microphones do not need it.

The BOMGE mini 2 is the most portable, since it is small, light and powered over USB. Desk boards need more space and often a wall adapter. Pack cables in a pouch and bring a spare USB lead, because a failed cable is the most common travel problem.

faq.q: Are bundles good for small desks?
faq.a: They are compact and complete, but the microphone is entry level. A bundle is a sensible way to test an idea cheaply, and the microphone is the first thing worth replacing when the show grows. If you already own a microphone, a bare board gives better value.
